description: The far end calls in, the edge bridges to the backend, and audio flows both ways: the backend hears the caller's 600 Hz and the caller hears the backend's 1000 Hz. The caller hangs up.
The backend ends the call; the BYE reaches the far end.
The far end gives up while the backend is ringing; the CANCEL reaches the backend.
The backend answers 486. The edge does not pass the failure back: it answers with the fallback, which in the bench is a 1400 Hz tone and an X-Fallback-Reason response header, then hangs up.
The backend declines with 603; the caller gets the fallback.
The backend rings past the edge's ring timeout (6 s in the bench); the caller gets the fallback.
The backend address doesn't respond at all (the edge routes user "unreachable" to a TEST-NET address); the caller gets the fallback once the ring timeout passes.
X- headers from the far end reach the backend unchanged.

The backend asks for a blind transfer with a REFER. The edge ends the REFER itself (202, NOTIFY, releases the backend) and places the transfer to the runner's target, carrying the caller's X- headers. The caller hears the backend, then the target; the target hears the caller.
RFC 2833 digits pass through the edge in both directions.
A far end offering only PCMU gets PCMU end to end.
A far end offering only PCMA gets PCMA end to end.
A far end offering only G.722 gets G.722. Skipped unless the run declares codec:g722: the bench's FreeSWITCH image has no G.722 module and the runner has no G.722 codec yet.
With the edge's session limit lowered to 4 (two bridged calls), a third concurrent call is refused with 503 and never reaches the backend. The limit is restored afterwards.
The edge answers OPTIONS with 200 while it has capacity (what a SIP proxy's dispatcher probes).
The backend echoes the caller's audio; the caller hears its own 600 Hz back through the edge.
